How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Perception of external (exteroceptive) and internal (interoceptive) sensory information is critical for a coherent sense of self, others, and the world. Perception depends on the accuracy and precision of sensory beliefs. Predictive processing models propose that altered sensory beliefs contribute to schizophrenia-spectrum disorders (SZ). However, exteroception and interoception are commonly assessed with separate paradigmatic and analysis schemes. We use a Heart Rate Discrimination (HRD) paradigm and Bayesian modeling to assess perceptual accuracy and precision during exteroceptive and interoceptive processing in SZ, and test associations with clinical variables.

Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale. Hierarchical Bayesian models estimated threshold (bias) and slope (precision), with Bayes factors assessing group difference credibility.

Participants were less biased and more precise during exteroceptive trials, without evidence of credible group differences in bias. SZ participants had less precise perceptual beliefs overall (BF10=6.74) with no credible group-by-condition interaction. Across all participants, higher interoceptive bias was associated with greater Not-Distracting of internal bodily signals (r=.21, 95% CrI [0.005, 0.41]), and lower interoceptive precision was associated with greater selfreported Body Listening (r=.40, 95% CrI [.08, .67]). Among SZ, lower interoceptive bias was associated with greater positive symptom severity (r=-.29, 95% CrI [-.54, -.01]).

Sensory beliefs are less precise in SZ. Further, biased interoceptive beliefs relate to psychotic symptoms and subjective bodily awareness. Interventions increasing precision and reducing bias of sensory beliefs may improve psychosis.

MANUSCRIPT WORD COUNT

3,996 / 4,000 1.

INTRODUCTION

Interoception is the reception, sensation, and perception of sensory signals originating from within the body, including air hunger, gastric fullness, bladder distention, and heart rate. 1, 2 As a broad domain, interoception has been further parcellated to capture distinct aspects of interoceptive sensory processing, including interoceptive awareness, accuracy, and precision. 3 Increasingly, these interoceptive constructs are understood within inferential frameworks, wherein perceptual judgments reflect the integration of noisy sensory evidence with prior beliefs about bodily states. 4 As interoception is increasingly recognized for its role in reality construction, emotional awareness, and salience attribution, [5] [6] [7] it has been the focus of recent research aiming to understand how the body perceives itself, and what implications this may have for neuropsychiatric illness. Cardiac interoception-"cardioception"-paradigms are commonly used to test interoceptive beliefs, given the ease of cardiac data collection and their modulation by sympathetic nervous system activation. [8] [9] [10] These include heartbeat-counting, heartbeat-tapping, and heart rate discrimination tasks, [11] [12] [13] each examining different aspects of cardioceptive processing. Heartbeat tracking paradigms ask participants to report counted or estimated cardiac signals but are susceptible to response bias. 14, 15 Conversely, heart rate discrimination paradigms require participants to compare cardiac signals with external (e.g., visual or auditory) stimuli. 16 While these task types are not completely independent, they measure largely different phenomena, with discrimination paradigms offering methodological strengths over tracking paradigms despite being more difficult to administer. 17, 18 Critically, discrimination paradigms generate psychometric functions that quantify bias and precision under experimentally-controlled uncertainty. The additional inclusion of exteroceptive comparison conditions allows examination of the specificity of perceptual deficits in sensory processing during such paradigms. Schizophrenia-spectrum disorders (SZ) offer a unique clinical lens through which to study and understand interoceptive abilities due to their symptomatologic profiles that have significant theoretical overlap with reported consequences of interoceptive deficits. Individuals with SZ can display symptoms spanning positive (i.e., delusions, hallucinations), negative (i.e., emotional blunting, anhedonia), and general (i.e., cognitive dysfunction, salience misattribution) domains. 19 Intriguingly, many of these psychotic symptoms, including delusions, hallucinations, alexithymia, deficits in emotional embodiment, and dissociative experiences, are tightly linked to interoceptive processing dysfunction and self-disturbances. [20] [21] [22] [23] Indeed, experimental and survey-based research in this clinical population has identified deficits in interoceptive accuracy, awareness, and precision compared to non-clinical cohorts. 21, [24] [25] [26] Taken together, existing evidence suggests altered interoceptive functioning in SZ, and predictive processing models of psychosis suggest that abnormalities in perceptual precision may extend across sensory domains rather than being specific to interoception. 27 However, research characterizing cardioceptive beliefs in SZ is sparse. Previous SZ studies have primarily used heartbeat-counting tasks and self-report measures, 21, 25, 26 while only one has used the HRD task, without the hierarchical modeling approach employed here. 24 Studying interoceptive functioning within a hierarchical Bayesian framework offers several advantages. Rather than treating individual threshold and slope estimates as fixed observations, hierarchical models use trial-level responses to estimate individual-and group-level parameters simultaneously, accounting for uncertainty in parameter estimates and allowing partial pooling across participants. This approach has demonstrated improved statistical power compared to conventional two-stage analyses, particularly with fewer trials or smaller samples. 28 Although Bayesian approaches have been used to study interoception in other psychiatric populations, they have not been applied to cardiac interoceptive psychophysics in SZ. 29 With this context, the present study aimed to build on prior literature exploring cardioceptive beliefs in individuals with SZ. By leveraging a cardioceptive Heart Rate Discrimination (HRD) task, we tested cardioceptive psychophysics and perceptual beliefs using hierarchical Bayesian modeling in individuals with SZ and healthy comparisons. We focused on the HRD-derived threshold (α; point of subjective equality; bias) and slope (β; precision around the point of subjective equality) variables as computational markers of perceptual bias and precision, respectively, across interoceptive and exteroceptive domains. Further, we compared taskderived interoceptive bias and interoceptive precision with self-reported interoceptive awareness to unite multiple subdomains of interoceptive processing within this clinical population. Specifically, we tested the hypotheses that (1) individuals with SZ would show altered perceptual bias and lower precision compared to HC; (2) these deficits would be more striking in interoceptive compared to exteroceptive conditions; and (3) HRD performance would be associated with self-reported interoceptive awareness. We further explored associations between interoceptive functioning and clinical symptoms of SZ.

2. METHODS AND MATERIALS

>METHODS AND MATERIALS

2.1. Study design and participants

Ninety participants (whose demographics and recruitment procedures have been reported previously) 30 were invited to participate in a cross-sectional study of individuals with and without schizophrenia-spectrum disorders (SZ). Inclusion criteria for all study participants included age 18-50 years, no history of cardiovascular or neurologic diagnoses, ability to communicate in English, and normal vision. All participants provided written informed consent to participate in the study and were compensated as approved by the Vanderbilt University Medical Center Institutional Review Board (#231058).

Forty-five participants with SZ were recruited from ongoing studies, with diagnoses confirmed via the Structured Clinical Interview for Diagnosis of DSM-5 Disorders (SCID-5; n=32 schizophrenia, n=8 schizophreniform disorder, and n=5 schizoaffective disorder). 31 We recorded duration of psychotic symptoms and antipsychotic medications, standardized to chlorpromazine equivalents. Additionally, 45 participants without a history of any psychopathology or psychotropic medication use as confirmed by the SCID-5, were recruited from the community as healthy comparison (HC) participants. HC participants were matched to SZ participants in age, sex, and parental education, a proxy for socioeconomic status. 32 >Study procedures >Heart Rate Discrimination (HRD) task

2.2.1.1. Task overview

Cardioceptive beliefs were assessed via the Heart Rate Discrimination (HRD) task (Figure 1), which has been previously described 12 and used 24 in individuals with SZ. Participants completed a version of the HRD task with 100 trials, comprising interoceptive and exteroceptive conditions (50 trials each) randomly interleaved. Participants completed the task in five blocks, with breaks provided after every 20 trials, lasting approximately 24 minutes.

During interoceptive trials, participants attended to their cardiac sensations for five seconds, during which heart rate was recorded via pulse oximetry, and then decided if a series of auditory tones was faster or slower than their heart rate. During exteroceptive trials, participants listened to a first set of auditory tones for five seconds and then decided if a second series of tones of the same volume was faster or slower in rate than the first. Exteroceptive tones were unrelated to heart rate and served as a comparison condition for attention and temporal estimation.

Participants completed the HRD task using PsychoPy v3.2.3 to present auditory and visual stimuli. 33 Heart rate was recorded at 100 Hz using a Nonin 3012LP Xpod USB pulse oximeter with a Nonin 8000SM fingertip sensor on the nondominant fourth finger, which were kept still throughout the task.

2.2.1.2. Hierarchical Bayesian modeling

We used an adaptive Bayesian staircase algorithm known as Ψ during the HRD task to select the tone frequencies and subsequently fit a hierarchical Bayesian model to estimate posterior distributions of psychometric function parameters from the trial-by-trial data (see Supplemental Methods). 28 This psychometric function is defined as the probability of judging a feedback series of auditory tones to be faster than a reference stimulus (i.e., heart rate) and is dependent on the objective rate difference between the two stimuli (Figure 2). This psychometric function is modeled with three parameters: 1) threshold (i.e., bias), the rate difference between feedback tones and a participant's actual heart rate when they are perceived to be equal; 2) slope (i.e., precision), a measure that controls how quickly the probability of a particular response shifts as a function of increasing feedback tone frequencies; and 3) lapse rate, which captures inattention during the task and defines the upper and lower bounds of the psychometric function for each trial. Threshold and slope were modeled separately for each condition for each participant, while lapse rate was modeled per participant.

Threshold represents the rate difference at which the reference and comparison stimuli are perceived as equal, with values closer to zero generally indicating greater accuracy. The slope parameter is inversely related to the steepness of the psychometric curve, with higher values reflecting lower precision (i.e., greater uncertainty). Slope was modeled on a logarithmic scale and transformed to beats per minute (BPM) for descriptive reporting. Finally, lapse rate captures occasional responses inconsistent with the psychometric function, allowing response probabilities to deviate from their probabilistic asymptotes.

Across both conditions, 90% of trials were updated adaptively according to the Bayesian Ψ method to maximize information about the psychometric curve near threshold. The remaining 10% were fixed "catch" trials, ensuring that participants encountered stimulus differences outside the adaptive staircase even after convergence. Data cleaning and quality assurance procedures for HRD task data are described in detail in Supplemental Methods.

2.2.2. Self-reported interoceptive awareness

We asked participants about their self-reported interoceptive awareness with the Multidimensional Assessment of Interoceptive Awareness (MAIA), version 2. 34 The MAIA is a validated and widely used 37-item state-trait assessment of interoceptive awareness that spans several domains of interoceptive awareness via its eight subscales (Noticing, Not-Distracting, Not-Worrying, Attention Regulation, Emotional Awareness, Self-Regulation, Body Listening, and Trusting). 35 Each item is scored on a 6-point Likert scale from 0 (Never) to 5 (Always), with higher scores representing better self-reported interoceptive awareness, and items are averaged to produce subscale scores.

2.2.3. Psychotic symptomatology

Psychotic symptomatology was assessed for all SZ participants by a trained rater using the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS). 36 The PANSS is a semi-structured interview that assesses the degree of symptomatology in positive, negative, and general domains for the preceding two weeks. The PANSS comprises three subscales: Positive, Negative, and General; each item is scored on a scale of 1-7, with higher scores reflecting more severe symptomatology. The PANSS is a validated and commonly used measure for capturing psychotic symptomatology. 37

2.2.4. Premorbid cognitive capacity

The Wechsler Test of Adult Reading (WTAR) was administered to all participants. 38 The WTAR provides a measure of cognitive ability that is resistant to cognitive decline found in some individuals with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders and is thus useful for estimating premorbid cognitive abilities in clinical populations. 39 Participants are asked to pronounce irregularlyspelled English words, with higher scores representing higher intelligence quotient (IQ).

2.5. Statistical analysis

All data were analyzed in R (R Core Team, 2019) using RStudio, version 2023.9.1.494. 40 Student's t-tests and Fisher's exact tests were used to evaluate group differences in continuous and categorical variables, respectively. Correction for multiple comparisons among MAIA scores was performed using the Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate (FDR) method.

To test our primary hypothesis that SZ participants would demonstrate deficits in bias (i.e., threshold) and precision (i.e., slope), particularly during interoceptive trials, we fit a hierarchical Bayesian model to the raw trial data from all participants, estimating five parameters per person: threshold and slope for both interoception and exteroception, and lapse rate across all conditions. Our primary model estimated lapse rate for each participant, while two additional models were fit as sensitivity analyses: one with lapse rate fixed at 0.02, consistent with the value assumed during adaptive Ψ staircasing and previous simulations, 28 and one including age and sex as covariates while estimating lapse rate (see Supplemental Methods). Hierarchical modeling allowed group-level parameter estimation simultaneously with individual-level estimation via partial pooling. The code to define the model was adapted from GitHub (https://github.com/embodied-computation-group/Cardioception). 41 We then computed the posterior distributions of group differences, condition differences, and group-by-condition interactions; we characterized these distributions by their means, 95% credible intervals, and posterior probabilities. Contrasts involving slope were calculated on the logarithmic scale, while group-level estimates were transformed to BPM for descriptive reporting. We additionally calculated Bayes factors (BF10) using the ratio of prior and posterior densities at zero to quantify evidence for group differences and interactions. Model comparisons were evaluated using the leave-one-out information criterion (LOOIC), with Pareto-k diagnostics used to assess the reliability of the estimates. Results from the primary model are presented in the main text, while sensitivity analyses are presented in Supplemental Results.

Secondly, to test our hypothesis that task-based interoceptive performance would be associated with self-reported interoceptive awareness across all participants, we fit multivariate normal models to examine associations between estimated psychometric parameters and MAIA scores, controlling for age, sex, and group. We additionally examined associations between task performance and psychotic symptom severity among SZ participants, controlling for age and sex. Parameter estimates from the hierarchical model carry meaningful uncertainty at the individual level (i.e., participants with fewer effective trials or noisier response patterns yield wider posterior distributions). Thus, these models accounted for uncertainty in individual parameter estimates when examining their associations with clinical and self-reported measures.

For each model, we report the posterior mean correlation coefficient (r), its 95% credible interval, and the posterior probability that the coefficient is positive. Associations whose 95% credible intervals excluded zero were considered credible; associations where the interval included zero, but the posterior probability exceeded 90% in either direction, are noted as preliminary. We did not apply formal post hoc correction for multiple comparisons to these association models; we instead rely on the 95% credible intervals and interpret results based on posterior uncertainty rather than binary thresholds.

3. RESULTS

>RESULTS

3.1. Group differences in demographic, clinical, and cognitive variables

One enrolled SZ participant did not complete the HRD task. We additionally excluded three participants (2 SZ, 1 HC) who completed <80% of trials or who responded 'Faster/Slower' for <20% or >80% of trials, implying a lack of task understanding. We further removed five SZ participants' interoceptive data and two SZ participants' exteroceptive data after visual inspection suggested random responses or incorrect mapping of 'Faster/Slower' responses (plots included in Supplemental Results). In total, data from 81 participants (44 HC, 37 SZ) were included for analysis in the interoception condition, and data from 84 participants (44 HC, 40 SZ) were included for analysis in the exteroceptive condition.

Group-level demographic, cognitive, clinical, and self-reported information is reported in Table 1. No statistically significant differences between HC and SZ were observed in age, sex, parental education, or race (all p>.05). However, the SZ group had significantly lower premorbid IQ (p<.05). In the SZ group, 63% were taking antipsychotic medication (CPZ equivalents: M=427mg, SD=313mg).

3.2. Group differences in HRD performance: Heart rate

Across the HRD task, SZ participants had a significantly higher basal heart rate (77.8 versus 72.1 beats per minute [BPM], t(75)=-2.55, p=.013, Table 2).

3.3. Group differences in HRD performance: Threshold

Across both groups, there was a credible difference in threshold between conditions, such that the threshold was closer to zero in the exteroceptive condition (HC: -1.30 BPM; SZ: -1.74 BPM) compared to the interoceptive condition (HC: -9.17 BPM; SZ: -7.03 BPM; mean difference = -6.58 BPM, 95% CrI [-9.02, -4.18]; Table 2). There was, however, no credible group difference in threshold across both conditions (mean difference = 0.85 BPM, 95% CrI [-1.70, 3.54], BF10=0.14), nor was there a credible group-by-condition interaction (mean difference = 2.57 BPM, 95% CrI [-2.32, 7.61], BF10=0.19). These results suggest similar task thresholds between participants in both groups, with all participants being more biased during interoceptive than exteroceptive trials (Figure 3A).

3.4. Group differences in HRD performance: Precision

As with threshold, we found that both groups were more precise with responses during exteroceptive than interoceptive trials (mean log slope difference = 0.494, 95% CrI [0.341, 0.651], Table 2). Here, we did observe a credible group difference across both conditions, such that SZ participants had lower overall precision (i.e., greater slope) than HC participants (mean log slope difference = 0.251, 95% CrI [0.053, 0.449], BF10=6.74). When examining each condition separately, greater slope in SZ was credibly observed during exteroceptive trials (mean difference = 0.357, 95% CrI [0.090, 0.612], BF10=8.71), while a smaller noncredible difference in the same direction was observed during interoceptive trials (mean difference = 0.145, 95% CrI [-0.092, 0.389], BF10=0.51). We did not find compelling evidence for a group-bycondition interaction (mean difference = -0.213, 95% CrI [-0.525, 0.096], BF10=0.55; Figure 3B). Results were largely consistent in sensitivity analyses using a fixed lapse rate and controlling for age and sex (see Supplemental Results).

3.5. Group differences in self-reported interoceptive awareness

Group-level self-reported interoceptive awareness is reported in Table 3. No statistically significant group difference was observed in overall self-reported interoceptive awareness (MAIA total; p=.08). At the subscale level, however, SZ participants reported significantly lower scores on the Not-Worrying subscale (pFDR=.032), indicating greater distress or concern related to bodily sensations. No other MAIA subscales differed significantly between groups after correction for multiple comparisons.

3.6. Condition-specific parameter associations with self-reported measures of interoception

Next, we were interested in understanding how task-derived interoceptive beliefs related to selfreported interoceptive awareness across our whole sample, controlling for age, sex, and group. We found that greater interoceptive slope (i.e., lower precision) was credibly associated with greater self-reported Body Listening (r=.40, 95% CrI [.08, .67]). A similar, but less credible, association was observed with greater Noticing (r=.20, 95% CrI [-.12, .51]). We also found a credible relationship between interoceptive threshold and self-reported Not-Distracting (r=0.21, 95% CrI [0.005, 0.41]), implying that having a bias towards overestimating one's heart rate is associated with tendencies to not suppress bodily sensations.

3.7. Condition-specific parameter associations with symptom severity

We finally examined symptom-behavior relationships among SZ participants. From our modeling, we found a credible association between interoceptive threshold and positive symptoms (r=-.290, 95% CrI [-.541, -.009]; Table 4). This suggests that greater positive symptom severity was associated with more underestimation of one's heart rate (that is, more negative interoceptive threshold). Additionally, we observed preliminary associations between greater exteroceptive slope and negative (r=.351, 95% CrI [-.027, .673]) and general symptom severity (r=.283, 95% CrI [-.083, .603]), although neither credible interval excluded zero. No other symptom domains had credible associations with task performance (Table 4).

4. DISCUSSION

The current study employed a paradigm designed to estimate bias and precision of interoceptive and exteroceptive beliefs and examined group differences between SZ and HC, associations with self-reported interoceptive awareness, and clinical symptoms. We observed evidence of reduced precision in SZ, in the context of similar task bias, suggesting that SZ participants had greater uncertainty about their perceptual beliefs. Furthermore, greater interoceptive slope (i.e., lower precision) was associated with greater subjective Body Listening, and to a lesser extent Noticing, suggesting that greater attention to bodily signals may in fact be related to less precise perceptual beliefs. Finally, we observed a credible association between interoceptive threshold and positive symptom severity, suggesting that less accurate interoceptive beliefs may relate to psychotic experiences.

The current study advances beyond existing interoception work in SZ by using an HRD task with rigorous hierarchical Bayesian modeling. One previous study has used this task in psychosis, reporting no group differences in signed threshold but identifying a group-bycondition interaction in absolute threshold, indicating greater magnitudes of interoceptive overor underestimation in the clinical cohort. 24 Our findings similarly demonstrated no credible group differences in signed threshold, although we did not directly examine absolute threshold. Comparing our SZ clinical cohort with this previous study, our population had more severe positive symptoms, less severe negative symptoms, and lower medication doses. Additionally, we used posterior distributions directly from the hierarchical model to compare groups, accounting for uncertainty in parameter estimates and allowing for partial pooling across participants. Future studies should standardize reporting of signed and absolute threshold measures to facilitate comparisons across cohorts.

Results from the current study can be understood through the predictive processing framework, 27 which highlights the integration of top-down prior expectations with bottom-up sensory information to inform self-perception. This model suggests that interoception can be less precise if either the sensory inputs are noisy, the prior beliefs about interoceptive precision are more uncertain, or both. 12, 42 Here, we see that SZ participants had similar accuracy on the task as HC but displayed greater slope values. Although there was a non-credible interaction, group differences were most credible for precision of exteroceptive beliefs. This finding is consistent with predictive processing models of psychosis, which posit that altered weighting of sensory information and prior beliefs may contribute to perceptual disturbances in SZ. 43 In this model, both interoceptive (e.g., racing heart) and exteroceptive (e.g., auditory rhythms) information may be processed with greater uncertainty. Importantly, our task cannot distinguish whether greater slope reflects noisier sensory information, altered prior expectations, or other perceptual processes. Interestingly, greater slope was associated with greater subjective Body Listening on the MAIA, while more negative interoceptive thresholds were associated with greater positive symptom severity on the PANSS.

While our results fit within the predictive processing model of psychosis, they differ from a recent study examining behavior on this task with an array of mental health symptoms in a large, non-clinical cohort. 44 This study found that interoceptive accuracy and precision were broadly unrelated to affective symptoms or attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and somatic symptoms. They were also unrelated to MAIA scores. Our current findings suggest that taskderived perceptual parameters may relate to specific facets of subjective interoceptive awareness, although these associations remain exploratory. Indeed, it could be that more serious mental health disorders allow for detection of these relationships that are obscured in heterogeneous non-clinical samples. However, differences in samples and modeling approaches may also contribute to these findings. Sensitivity analyses conducted in our own data (e.g., examination of different lapse rates, inclusion of covariates) showed a largely consistent pattern of group differences, although uncertainty remains surrounding the weaker interoceptive and clinical associations. While this could be due in part to our modest sample size, it highlights the need for continued research in this area and refinement of tasks and models for measuring perceptual beliefs.

A key limitation is our modest sample size. The HRD task, and the interoceptive portion specifically, is mentally challenging and taxing; thus, a subset of our SZ participants showed evidence of task misunderstanding, and we excluded these data. Future studies should confirm task understanding before recorded trials begin, particularly in clinical cohorts with cognitive difficulties. Larger samples may help detect subtle group differences despite data exclusions.

Another limitation of this study is that, without specific hypotheses of which self-reports and symptom subscales would associate with parameters, these data were not included in the original hierarchical Bayesian models. Although our multivariate normal models accounted for uncertainty in individual parameter estimates, the exploratory nature and number of associations examined leave their interpretability uncertain. Future studies should prioritize hypothesis-driven analyses that incorporate these relationships within hierarchical models and evaluate their robustness to multiple comparisons. Additionally, we examined associations between self-reported interoception and estimated parameters in the whole study cohort, but it is plausible that these parameters have different interpretations in clinical and healthy populations.

Additionally, differences in the cardiovascular system outside of the realm of interoception may obscure our results. We saw a significant difference between groups in average heart rate during interoceptive trials, and it is well-known that psychiatric medications affect cardiometabolic health in populations taking antipsychotic medications. 45 Additionally, differences in tobacco use between groups (Table 1) may contribute to differences in cardiovascular or autonomic functioning. Heart rate is easier to detect when it is elevated, 46 and it is possible that this affects HRD results when comparing groups. Although heart rate was included in a sensitivity analysis of group differences, we did not additionally adjust the exploratory threshold-positive symptom association for heart rate, given our modest sample size. Future studies may also integrate different interoceptive modalities to compare across body systems given these known cardiac effects.

Regarding our hypothesis that individuals with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders would show reduced accuracy and precision, particularly during interoception, we did not see credible group differences in threshold, though we found greater slope (i.e., lower precision) in SZ, with the strongest evidence during exteroceptive trials. Although interoceptive slope followed a similar pattern, evidence for this group difference was weaker, and we did not find a credible group-bycondition interaction. For our hypothesis that HRD performance would be associated with selfreported interoceptive abilities, we found that greater slope was associated with greater Body Listening across participants, suggesting that subjective attention to bodily signals may not necessarily reflect more precise perceptual beliefs. Finally, we observed a credible association between more negative interoceptive thresholds and greater positive symptom severity among SZ participants, although this exploratory relationship requires further investigation. Future studies should prioritize larger sample sizes and hierarchical modeling of hypothesized task parameter-self-report and symptom relationships to better characterize the behavioral meaning of these parameters. Participants completed a 100-trial version of the task consisting of 50 interoceptive trials, where participants decided if a series of auditory tones was faster or slower than their heart rate (A, left), randomly interleaved with 50 exteroceptive or control trials, where participants decided which of two series of auditory tones was faster (B, right).

SUPPLEMENTAL METHODS

The Heart Rate Discrimination (HRD) task and the Ψ method One advantage of the HRD task over other commonly used measures of cardiac interoception is the ability to leverage an adaptive, Bayesian algorithm to optimize stimuli based on the participant's previous responses. This Ψ or staircase algorithm selects a "HR," or a "change in auditory rate from recorded heart rate," that maximizes information to be gained on a trial-bytrial basis. To do this the algorithm assumes that the trial by trial data of the HRD task can be described by a psychometric function that relates the probability in judging a feedback auditory tone to be faster than one's heart rate with the objective rate difference between the two stimuli (Figure 2, main text). This function is modeled with three parameters: (1) threshold (α; i.e., bias), the rate difference between the reference and comparison stimuli when they are perceived to be equal; (2) slope (β; i.e., precision), a measure that controls how quickly the probability of a particular response shifts as a function of increasing feedback tone frequencies; and (3) lapse rate (λ), which captures inconsistent responses during the task and defines the upper and lower bounds of the psychometric function. In modeling task performance, threshold and imprecision were estimated separately for each condition (interoception, exteroception), while lapse rate was estimated once per participant. Lapse rate estimation ensures accurate bounds of the psychometric curve. Estimating lapse does not assume a participant will perform at perfect accuracy, accounting for brief lapses in attention; without this, predictions of imprecision can be inflated.

The ψ method also returns estimates for the slope and threshold of the psychometric function, derived from the probability distribution it tracks across trials. However, using these point estimates as data for group-level inference is problematic because it ignores the uncertainty of each individual estimate and prevents information from being shared across participants. To address this, we propose to use hierarchical psychometric function models to fit the trial-wise data generated by the tasks, enabling joint estimation of parameters across individuals and conditions. This approach preserves uncertainty, enables principled pooling of information, and improves the robustness of group-level inference.

HRD data cleaning and quality assurance

To inspect data quality, we first observed the proportion of trials completed by each participant (Figure S1) and the overall proportion of 'Faster' responses across all trials (Figure S2), which we expected to be near 50% given the use of Ψ.

F igure S2.

Proportion of trials where participants selected that a first series of auditory tones (exteroception) or their resting heart rate (interoception) was faster than a subsequent presented series of auditory tones. Given the adaptive Ψ staircase method used, this proportion was expected to be around 50%, and significant deviations from this could imply a response bias or lack of effort or understanding of the task that could risk data quality. We imposed a requirement of this proportion to exist between 20-80%.

Additionally, for each participant in each condition, we inspected binned plots of the proportion of participant decisions of 'Faster' across the spectrum of frequency differences between recorded heart rate and presented tone (HR) (Figures S3 and S4). We expected binned plots to be roughly positively monotonic, where each bin has a higher proportion of 'Faster' responses.

Figure S3. Binned proportion of 'Faster' responses for SZ participants in both (A) exteroception and (B) interoception conditions with an inferred cumulative distribution function. Binned plots that were not roughly monotonic were further investigated using per-trial choice information.

A. SZ -exteroception B. SZ -interoception

For plots that were not positively monotonic, we additionally inspected decisions made across trials and HRs (Figures S5 and S6). This allowed us to visualize misunderstanding of task rules (i.e., if a participant responds consistently 'Faster' at negative HRs and 'Slower' at positive HRs) and lack of effort or attention (i.e., no clear separation in HRs between 'Faster' and 'Slower' responses). We excluded participants based on visual inspection if four authors agreed that the participant showed evidence of lack of effort or misunderstanding of the task based on their response patterns. Exclusions were made a condition-specific basis; a participant could have their interoceptive data excluded but their exteroceptive data included. All exclusions were finalized before model fitting. Bayesian models of cardiac interoception in psychosis Hierarchical Bayesian modeling Three hierarchical models were fit to the same dataset after exclusions were made. These models were constructed to rigorously test whether group differences were dependent on modeling choices or persisted throughout testing. Each model used the same sampler characteristics: 4 chains, 1000 tuning iterations, 1000 sampling iterations, target average proposal acceptance probability 0.95, and maximum binary tree steps of 12. Priors were empirically derived from an independent study using the HRD task. 1, 2 Priors were set equal across all participants, serving as a baseline assumption of no difference between groups. Thus, if a group difference appeared, it was due to evidence in the data itself and not biased by prior expectation of group differences. Because Models 1-3 are fit to the same dataset, they are be compared formally using information criteria as shown below. Model 4 serves as a sensitivity analysis and is not formally compared to the other three models. All models were written in Stan based on Github examples 3 and fit using the cmdstanr package in R.

Model 1: estimated lapse

This model estimated 10 parameters at the group level: α (threshold) and β (imprecision) for each group (SZ, HC) and condition (interoception, exteroception), and λ (lapse) for each group held constant across conditions. On an individual level, this model estimated threshold and imprecision for each condition and one lapse constant across both conditions. Lapse was estimated per individual and group to more accurately model imprecision, which can appear artificially inflated if it is assumed that an individual or group will have perfect performance at stimuli that are far from the perceptual threshold. By allowing performance in these areas to approach but not reach 100%, we account for lapses in attention, buttonpressing mistakes, and other sources of human more appropriately, allowing this lapse rate to vary on an individual and group basis.

Model 2: fixed lapse (2%)

With the Ψ staircase, trials concentrate near each participant's threshold by design, which leaves comparatively little information in the raw data about the lapse rate specifically. In order to determine if estimating lapse was solely responsible for a potential difference in imprecision between groups on a given condition, we fit an additional model that fixed lapse at 2%, a modeling choice that has previously been used for simulation in the literature. 1 Comparing Model 1 to Model 2 determines whether estimating lapse rather than fixing it changes the group comparison, i.e., whether the models' conclusions are an artifact of how lapse is handled. In this way, Model 2 serves as a sensitivity analysis of Model 1, the method that relies more heavily on the data for modeling output. This analysis followed a two stage process that 1) estimated model parameters given task data and 2) investigated relationships between these estimated model parameters and clinical and self-report interoceptive data. Traditional Pearson correlation treats model parameters as point estimates and does not account for their uncertainty, an important aspect of the Bayesian parameter. An effect of treating these estimates as absolute points rather than uncertain bands with a mean is attenuated correlation values. 5 To better account for parameter estimate uncertainty and maximize use of the Bayesian model output, a multivariate normal model was fit, which takes the mean parameter value and its standard deviation as inputs alongside clinical and self-report data and adjusting for covariates including age, sex, and diagnostic group. The model estimates the true value of the parameter within its range of likely values. 5 Outcomes of this model fit are reported with simple Pearson correlations with and without FDR correction for comparison separately for Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) scores (among SZ participants only) and Multidimensional Assessment for Interoceptive Awareness (MAIA) self-report (across both groups). Model 3: estimated lapse, age and sex covariates

Our sample is matched on age and sex, but these demographic variables could plausibly affect perceptual task performance independent of diagnosis. Like Model 1, Model 3 estimates lapse at the group and individual levels. It also adds standardized age and binary sex as covariates on threshold, imprecision, and lapse, estimating covariate effects and group effects simultaneously. As a result, the reported group means describe a male participant of mean age. This model assesses whether group differences survive adjustment for age and sex.

Model 4: estimated lapse, age, sex, and heart rate covariates

Groups differ on average heart rate (main text, 3.2). Antipsychotic medications are known to alter heart rate, which offers one route by which medication could affect task performance. 4 We did not use antipsychotic dose (CPZ) as a covariate because every control participant has a dose of zero; thus dose cannot be separated from group membership, whereas heart rate varies within both groups. Model 4 uses only the interceptive trials and includes heart rate as a covariate on top of age and sex from Model 3. For each participant, we averaged the heart rate recording during the listening phase of each interoceptive trial and standardized across all participants. Heart rate enters the model as a covariate on threshold and imprecision, but not lapse. This sensitivity analysis asks whether accounting for heart rate changes interoceptive group differences estimated in Model 3. Because this model uses only interoceptive trials, it cannot be formally compared to the other models.

Comparison of Models 1-4

Models 1-3 were formally compared because they were fit to the same task data after exclusion. The metrics of comparison of choice was leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO). LOO asks how well the model predicts each observation when that observation is left out. Rather than refitting the model once per observation, it reweights the results of a single full fit. A diagnostic called the Pareto-k value checks whether this approximation works for each observation; values above 0.7 mark observations that are influential enough to the overall estimation that its approximation fails, marking reliance on single observations and instability. Metrics were discussed between five authors and consensus was reached about which model performed the best and should be passed onto the second stage of analysis, described below.

Exclusions

A summary of all exclusions is included in Table S1. For a low completion rate, we excluded 2 SZ participants for interoception and 1 SZ participant for exteroception (Figure S1). For evidence of response bias, we excluded one HC participant's interoceptive data (Figure S2).

From visual inspection and discussion among authors, we excluded five additional SZ participants in the interoception condition and two additional SZ participants in the exteroception condition (Figures S3-S6). Three participants were excluded from both conditions; thus, their clinical and self-report data was also excluded.

The following sections are detailed separately for Models 1-3 to assess model design and fit: 1.

Prior predictive check. A prior predictive check, which involves simulating data from the priors alone, before the model incorporates evidence from the provided dataset, confirms that the priors cover plausible psychometric curves (Figures S7, S10, and S13). 2. Model fitting diagnostics. Convergence was assessed with four standard checks: 1) number of divergences, 2) R-hat, 3) effective sample size (ESS), and 4) Energy Bayesian Fraction of Missing Information (E-BFMI). Divergences assess whether a sampler failed to explore an area of parameter space, indicating that estimates may be biased. R-hat above 1.01, by convention, means the independent chains have not converged to the same distribution. ESS assesses the independent information in autocorrelated samples of a Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampler; an ESS above 400 is considered acceptable. E-BFMI measures how efficiently the sampler moves through the model's energy distribution; a value of > 0.2 is considered acceptable. Trace plots showing the 4 chains are displayed in Figures S8, S11, and S14.3. Posteriors. The posterior predictive check overlays model-implied response proportions on the observed binned data (Figures S9, S12, and S15). Because of partial pooling, the model treats each participant's estimate as a compromise between their own data and the group average, weighted by how noisy their own data is. Thus, the model is better able to capture and smooth over individual outliers that may distort the raw data.

Posterior estimates and contrasts with credible intervals are displayed in Tables 2 (main text), S2, and S3.

Model 1: estimated lapse 1. Prior predictive check: Shown in Figure S7. The simulated curves using prior distributions encompass the binned observed data. 2. Model fitting diagnostics: Trace plot shown in Figure S8 appears healthy with good mixing, which is corroborated by a maximum R-hat value of 1.0065. There were no divergent transitions, the minimum bulk sample size was 467, and the E-BFMI was 0.768, all falling in acceptable ranges and pointing to a good model fit. 3. Posteriors: Posterior distributions overlaid on priors are shown in Figure S9; Table 2 (main text) displays the group average parameter estimates and group contrast posteriors with 95% credible intervals.

Table S2. Group posteriors and contrasts of Model 2 alpha (threshold, BPM) and log beta (slope). Abbreviations: CrI = credible interval; HC = healthy comparison; SZ = schizophreniaspectrum.

Model 3: estimated lapse with age and sex covariates 1. Prior predictive check: Shown in Fig. S13. The simulated curves using prior distributions encompass the binned observed data. 2. Model fitting diagnostics: Trace plot shown in Fig S14 appears healthy with good mixing, which is corroborated by a maximum R-hat value of 1.0089. There were no divergent transitions, the minimum bulk sample size was 423, and the E-BFMI was 0.778, all falling in acceptable ranges and suggesting to a good model fit. 3. Posteriors: Posterior distributions overlaid on priors are shown in Fig. S15. Table S3 displays the group average parameter estimates and group contrast posteriors with 95% credible intervals.

Model comparison

Formal comparison of Models 1-3 is displayed in Table S4. The most significant difference between the models appeared in the number of Pareto-k's that were above 0.7. Models 1 and 3 had significantly better performance by this metric and slightly better performance by LOOIC.

Table S4. Model 1-3 comparison. Models run on the full task dataset post-exclusion were formally compared before selecting the best fitting model to proceed with stage 2 of analysis. For all metrics, a lower number signifies a better fit, but numbers separated by less than 2 standard errors are not clearly distinguishable. Model LOOIC LOOIC SE # Pareto-k > 0.7 1 5465.27 88.22 4 2 5476.03 87.10 131 3 5464.93 88.23 4 Abbreviations: LOOIC = Leave-One-Out Information Criterion, SE = standard error.

Given the statistically indistinguishable performance of Models 1 and 3, the simpler model (Model 1) was selected for progression into stage 2 of analysis with multivariate normal modeling of its estimated parameters and clinical and self-report variables.

Multivariate normal model: MAIA score relationsips with interoceptive parameters Estimated correlations between MAIA subscales and estimated interoceptive parameters from Model 1 are shown in Figure S18 and those whose 90% credible intervals exclude zero are include in Table 4, main text. Comparison of these relationships estimated from multivariate normal modeling to traditional Pearson correlations with and without FDR correction are presented in Table S6.

Figure 2.

Figure 2. Heart Rate Discrimination task group-level psychometric functions. Interoceptive and exteroceptive conditions were interleaved throughout the task, and a hierarchical Bayesian model estimated posterior distributions for threshold and imprecision in both conditions, and one lapse, on both individual and group levels. Group-level psychometric curves were constructed from group-level mean posteriors, where groups are represented by color (orange = SZ, blue = HC), and condition is represented by line type (interoception = dashed, exteroception = solid). Shaded bands show the 95% credible interval, which reflects uncertainty in the group-level estimate rather than variability between participants.

Figure 3.

Figure 3. Posterior distributions of group-level thresholds and imprecision. Full posterior distributions for both threshold/accuracy (A, top) and slope/precision (B, bottom) are displayed; individuals' mean estimates are represented below each respective group posterior distribution with box plots.

Figure S5.

FigureS5. Per-trial decisions in the SZ group across (A) exteroception and (B) interoception. This view of the raw data aided in exclusion decision-making when the binned decision plots were not roughly monotonic. Evidence of lack of task understanding throughout the task or lack of effort was inferred from poor separation of trial decisions across differences in presented tone BPM.
